notes: Hand-picked, because eBird Status & Trends marks most Indian birds as rare (799 of 1,390 species) and the automatic cut gives far too few. The list uses GBIF/eBird record counts for the whole country (November 2026, occurrence.csv), a second count for Delhi, Uttar Pradesh, Haryana, Rajasthan and Punjab to find what a north Indian trip really meets, plus birding knowledge. It covers a classic north India trip of two to three weeks: Delhi parks and gardens, Sultanpur and the Yamuna, Agra, Bharatpur and Keoladeo (storks, cranes, Sarus, Painted Stork, Spot-billed Pelican, Dusky Eagle-Owl, the winter ducks and raptors), Ranthambore and the Corbett lowlands, village and farmland birds (mynas, bulbuls, babblers, parakeets, doves, drongos, shrikes, kingfishers, bee-eaters, rollers), widespread waterbirds and waders, the common raptors and vultures, and the common winter visitors (wheatears, flycatchers, warblers, buntings, Rosy Starling). Widespread birds of the whole subcontinent are in too, such as Purple-rumped Sunbird. India has 85 endemic-status species in the database. Only four are in the country trip because a visitor on the northern route really meets them: Rufous-tailed Lark, Spot-breasted Fantail, Grey Junglefowl and Red Spurfowl (dry hills and open ground south of the Ganges, Ranthambore and the Aravallis). The chapter is thin on purpose. The other 81 belong to regional packs: the Western Ghats and south (about 40, from White-cheeked Barbet and Malabar Parakeet to the sholakilis and Nilgiri Woodpigeon), the Andaman and Nicobar islands (about 25), the Northeast and Himalaya (a handful, such as Bugun Liocichla and Mishmi Wren-Babbler), and the dry west and centre (Painted Spurfowl, Rock Bush-Quail, Tawny Lark, Great Indian Bustard, Forest Owlet, Jerdon's Courser). Left for the regional packs, by region. Himalaya and foothills: pheasants, monal, snowcocks, most laughingthrushes, fulvettas, forktails, redstarts, rosefinches, accentors, Wallcreeper, Great and Blue-throated Barbets, Grey Treepie, Crimson Sunbird, Hair-crested Drongo, Fulvous-breasted and Grey-capped Pygmy Woodpeckers, Pallas's Fish-Eagle. Northeast: hornbills, wren-babblers, pittas, Greater Adjutant, Bengal Florican, spiderhunters, broadbills, White-rumped Munia. Western Ghats and far south: the Malabar endemics, Loten's Sunbird, White-bellied Blue Flycatcher, Malabar Trogon, Nilgiri birds, Blue-faced Malkoha, Jerdon's Leafbird, Yellow-billed Babbler. Central India tiger forests: Mottled Wood-Owl, Painted Francolin, Forest Owlet, Collared Scops-Owl, Maroon Oriole. Kutch, Thar and the Gujarat coast: Greater Hoopoe-Lark, Desert and Bimaculated Larks, coursers, sandgrouse, Great Indian Bustard, Houbara, Demoiselle Crane, Lesser Flamingo, Western Reef-Heron, Crab-Plover, Variable and Desert Wheatears, Indian Skimmer, Sociable Lapwing, Sind Woodpecker, Caspian Tern. Andaman and Nicobar: all their endemics, Andaman Drongo, Andaman Coucal. Coast and sea: pelagic seabirds, boobies, frigatebirds, Pacific Reef-Heron, shore waders and plovers of the mudflats, Pacific Golden Plover. Winter vagrants and scarce migrants were left out on purpose. Pallid Harrier, Imperial Eagle and Common Crane are in because they are regular at Bharatpur and the Rajasthan wetlands. Left out because the photos in the library could not be identified with confidence (add back once reviewed): Sind Sparrow (sinspa1), Sykes's Warbler (sykwar2), Indian Spotted Eagle (inseag1), Streak-throated Swallow (sttswa2), Grey-throated Martin (gytmar1), Indian Scops Owl (insowl1), Dusky Crag Martin (duscrm1) and Savanna Nightjar (savnig1). Shared look_for texts exist for these already. Shaky photo picks, to check on /trip-photos: Himalayan Griffon (flight shots only), Red Junglefowl (photos look like feral fowl), Tawny Eagle, Laggar Falcon, Clamorous Reed Warbler, Brown Fish-Owl (two card photos only), Eastern Red-rumped Swallow (two card photos), Common Babbler, Large Grey Babbler, Asian Tit, White-eared Bulbul, Booted Warbler, Jungle Myna, Red-whiskered Bulbul.
